issues.issue: The extension operates only "to the extent such Collective Bargaining Agreement is not modified by, or inconsistent with" the Memorandum, but the Memorandum supplies no rule for deciding when a CBA term is "inconsistent" with it. Which of the two instruments controls on any disputed subject is therefore left to construction.

A "restated commitment" to "orderly, successful and efficient start-up and operations" states no measurable obligation and no consequence for failure. Whether it is an operative promise or mere preamble is open.

The "commitment to negotiate those issues arising out of the start-up and operations" at other facilities fixes no subject matter, timetable or standard of good faith. It is an agreement to agree whose enforceable content is undefined.

This clause applies the contract at "any new or rebuilt facility," but the May 16, 1992 side letter (c074) removes 43rd Street and the staging facility from all references to "new and rebuilt facilities." The two must be reconciled to know where the Memorandum-as-modified operates.

The permitted Edison practices are described generally ("technological innovations, methods of operation, scheduling practices and/or working conditions") and then illustrated by "e.g. palletization, tractor-trailer delivery to wholesalers, and card reader system." Whether the general words are confined to matters of the kind enumerated is a classic ejusdem generis question.

"[A]fter a period of 120 days" has no stated starting event — notice, commencement of negotiations, or announcement of the innovation. The trigger for compulsory interest arbitration is therefore indeterminate.

The paragraph is headed "The Contract Arbitrator" but its text terminates the "Merits Arbitrator," and "contract year" is nowhere defined. Which office may be terminated, and in what annual window, is uncertain on the face of the clause.

The Merits Arbitrator is given all grievance jurisdiction "except as otherwise provided herein," yet paragraph 7C (c033) preserves the Joint Standing Committee, Adjustment Board and Appeal Board as the deciding tribunals, and paragraph 2 also keeps a Status Quo Arbitrator. Which forum hears a given dispute cannot be settled from this clause alone.
No period is fixed within which the parties must "fail to reach agreement" before the AAA rules take over. When either side may invoke the AAA procedure is left open.

The clause selects a new Status Quo Arbitrator "pursuant to the procedure described in paragraph B above," but section 2 of the Memorandum contains no lettered paragraph B. The cross-reference is a mechanical error that leaves the selection procedure unidentified.
"[A]ll active NMDU RSHs employed by the Times" turns on the undefined word "active," which fixes no date and no employment status test. Who is inside the buyout class is therefore contestable.

This definition requires presence on the Group I list both at signing and at ratification, while Attachment B's eligibility clause (c053) requires only that the individual be on the list "effective the date of ratification." The two eligibility tests cannot both govern the same buyout class.

"[T]hese contributions shall be in lieu of and not in addition to those that would otherwise be called for by the Agreement" does not say whether the 450-FTE figure is a floor only, or also a ceiling displacing the CBA's per-shift-worked contribution obligation. The phrase governs the size of the employer's whole welfare obligation and reads both ways.

The clause fixes only that contributions are "based on the highest straight time scale" but states no number of shifts or weeks per year for employees who are no longer working. The amount of the post-buyout pension contribution is therefore not computable from the text.

The 45-day window commences "promptly after ratification," which fixes no date certain for the opening or closing of the offer. Later provisions (c026, c027) key operational rights to "closure of the forty-five (45) day buyout offer period," so the vagueness propagates.

The Times must add employees "necessary to reach 370 regular situations" but the only permitted source is Eligible Group I Employees who decline the buyout, a pool that may be too small. The clause does not say what happens if 370 cannot be reached from that source.

The 270-RSH floor applies only "[o]nce the replacement procedure has been completed," but the paragraph gives the procedure no completion event — it runs "during the term of this Agreement." When the floor attaches is therefore indeterminate.

The duty to replace absent RSHs turns on whether reporting numbers are "insufficient to satisfy specific manning requirements," a term used repeatedly but nowhere defined in the Memorandum. Whose manning standard governs is left open.

Promotion is required only where "necessary to comply ... with specific manning requirements," an undefined benchmark. The circumstances triggering a mandatory promotion cannot be identified from the text.

"[F]ollowing discussion with the Union" imposes a precondition of unspecified content, timing or effect before The Times exercises its discretion. Whether a single notice satisfies it, and what follows if it does not occur, is unstated.

The proviso barring consolidation of situations "in which one run constitutes the entire day's or night's work for a shift on three or more shifts each week" is opaque as to what counts as "one run" and how shifts are counted. The scope of the limit on consolidation is the whole of its content.

The clause permits reorganization of "all existing daily West Side Direct routes, including both daily and Sunday routes" and then a "fifty percent (50%)" reduction yielding exactly thirteen routes, figures that do not reconcile with treating Sunday routes as part of the daily total. Whether the 50% cap or the fixed route/assignment numbers controls is ambiguous.

The reorganization is stated to be "subject only to the limitation" of a forty-route minimum, yet the May 16, 1992 Saturday Night Bulldog letter (c075) imposes a further limitation freezing forty current finishing times. The word "only" cannot be squared with that letter.

Moving SNBD start times to no later than 4:00 p.m. after Edison opens sits against the side letter (c075) freezing the forty current finishing times for those routes. Whether shift length may be lengthened, or the finishing times move with the start times, is unresolved between the two.
"[D]aily Bulldog routes" is not defined and its boundary against the separately treated Saturday Night Bulldog routes is unclear. Whether Saturday routes count toward the two/four minima is open.

Cash collections continue "on recovery routes," a category the Memorandum never defines, and the permitted "alternate billing system" is left wholly unspecified. The boundary between eliminated and continued collections is uncertain.

After enumerating strikes, job actions and acts honoring picket lines against named categories, the clause sweeps in "any other acts that interfere with the Publisher's operations or the production or sale of its products or services." How far that catch-all extends beyond the enumerated kinds of conduct is an ejusdem generis question.

Release is available "after five (5) working days," but the saving proviso measures the non-complying party's time to move to vacate by "that five (5) day period." The two counting rules are inconsistent within one sentence.

The release mechanism runs off awards of the Joint Standing Committee, Adjustment Board and Appeal Board, while paragraph 2 (c008) vests all grievance resolution in the Merits Arbitrator "except as otherwise provided herein." Whether a Merits Arbitrator award triggers this release cannot be answered from either clause alone.

The clause states a fixed resulting scale of $952.80, but the cost-of-living provision (c040) directs adjustments "beginning on March 31, 1992" on a new January-to-January index. The stated dollar result and the COLA-adjusted scale cannot both be true.

A resulting scale of $986.80 is fixed for March 31, 1994, the same date on which c040 requires a cost-of-living adjustment to the scale. Whether the COLA is on top of, or already embedded in, the stated figure is unresolved between the two clauses.

A resulting scale of $1020.80 is fixed for March 31, 1995, while c040 requires a cost-of-living adjustment effective the same date. The stated figure and the COLA provision cannot both be applied without construction.

The reopener sends "the matter" to binding arbitration without saying whether the arbitrator's remit is wages alone or the whole reopener package, and "the then current scale" is not fixed to a date. The scope of the interest arbitration is therefore contestable.

The sentence is grammatically incomplete — "reapportion the contributions due on those increases between its pension plan and its health and welfare plan the total pension (8%) and health and welfare (7.68%) plan contributions made by The Times" — so it cannot be told whether the Union may reapportion only the contributions attributable to the wage increases or the entire 15.68% of contributions. The missing words are the whole subject of the right conferred.

A reapportionment that raises the welfare percentage sits against paragraph 3.A.(3) (c015), which fixes health and welfare contributions at a 450-Full-Time-Equivalent minimum "in lieu of and not in addition to" what the Agreement would otherwise require. How a percentage-based reapportionment operates on an FTE-based fixed obligation is not addressed.

The clause lists adjustment dates beginning March 31, 1994 but the proviso speaks of "all such adjustments beginning on March 31, 1992," a date not in the list, and omits March 31, 1996 altogether. The internal mismatch leaves the set of adjusted years uncertain.

Ratification is required "by each of the parties" with no deadline, no procedure and no statement of what happens if one party fails to ratify. Because the buyout periods and other obligations run from ratification, the omission has operative consequences.

Attachment A limits eligibility to RSHs on the "Steady Situation list ... currently holding positions," while paragraph 3.A of the Memorandum (c011) offers the buyout to "all active NMDU RSHs employed by the Times, including foremen." The two eligibility descriptions do not coincide, and the Memorandum says the Attachments contain the governing terms.
"[I]nterest at prevailing market interest rates" fixes no index, term or measuring date for the annuity purchase. The value of the alternative to a lump sum is therefore indeterminate.

The unpaid balance is directed to "the employee's estate," but the Notice of Termination form the employee must sign (c052) invites him to name a person to whom "the remaining amount of my buyout shall be paid." Estate versus named designee cannot both control the same balance.

The cross-reference to "Paragraph 3-A-(3) and 3-A-(5)" is unreliable because the subparagraphs of paragraph 3.A are mis-numbered in the Memorandum (the sequence runs 1), 2), 3), then 5), 6), 7)). Which numbered promises this Attachment incorporates has to be worked out against c015 and c017.

The employee is made to surrender "his or her contractual guarantee of employment," a guarantee this Attachment never identifies — it may mean the Appendix A employment guarantees, the CBA's job security, or both. What is being given up is left to construction.
The 45-day period runs "promptly after ratification of this Agreement," fixing neither the opening date nor the closing date of the offer. "Promptly" is the only measure supplied.
